item.title: How to Choose an AI Agent Platform for Your Team
item.description: A vendor-agnostic evaluation checklist for AI agent platforms: pilot-failure data, six evaluation criteria, governance pressure, and a scorecard you can reuse.
item.content:encoded:
Construct gives your team a live browser, a sandbox terminal, workspace files, connected apps, memory you can correct, and published plan limits in one workspace from $9 a month, which makes it the quickest platform to run this checklist against. Many products sold as agents cannot pass it: Gartner estimates only about 130 of the thousands of vendors marketing "agentic AI" are genuinely agentic (Digital Applied, agent-washing scorecard).

This guide gives you six criteria that predict whether a platform survives contact with real work, the governance rules now attached to that decision, and a scorecard you can apply to any product on your shortlist. The criteria are vendor-agnostic. Under each one we show how Construct answers it, because for founders and small teams it is the platform we recommend piloting first: it acts on every surface a real job needs, keeps the work in files your team can open, and costs $9 to try.

Why run this checklist on Construct first?

  • Every execution surface in one task. A live browser, a sandbox terminal, workspace files, connected apps, and its own email address, without stitching tools together.
  • Work that survives the session. Finished work is saved to workspace files as it is produced, so a run that stops at step 30 still leaves steps 1 to 29 behind.
  • Memory you can inspect and correct. Open what Construct has learned, fix one stale fact, or forget it, without wiping the rest.
  • Reach for internal systems. A live integration catalog for common business apps, plus custom MCP tools for systems with no public integration.
  • A team workspace without seats. Owner, Admin, and Member roles, no member limit, and usage that draws on the owner's plan.
  • Published limits at a fixed monthly price. Lite is $9 (2 agents, 50 steps per task, 3 scheduled tasks), Starter $59, Pro $299 with a 7-day trial, with no per-message billing.

Why most AI agent pilots never reach production

Gartner forecasts that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027 due to escalating costs, unclear business value, or inadequate risk controls (Gartner, press release, cited via Digital Applied's agent-washing scorecard). Gartner Senior Director Analyst Anushree Verma named the underlying problem directly: "most agentic projects today are early-stage experiments driven by hype," which blinds organizations to the real cost and complexity of deploying agents at scale.

The failure pattern is not random. Digital Applied's failure framework names the usual causes: scope creep, where a bounded automation absorbs new requirements until it becomes an open-ended system nobody scoped for; data quality, when an agent tested on clean samples meets messy production records; and security, integration, and ownership gaps (Digital Applied, AI agent failure framework). It publishes no dataset behind its percentages, so treat the list as a checklist rather than a measurement: scope and data readiness are the two to check first.

This is also an active buying decision for most teams, not a settled one. Only 17% of organizations had deployed AI agents as of 2026, while more than 60% expect to deploy within two years, per Gartner's CIO survey (Digital Applied, agent-washing scorecard). The criteria below are aimed at that gap: the difference between a platform that produces a good pilot and one that keeps producing good results after the third team starts depending on it.

The AI agent evaluation checklist: 6 criteria that separate a pilot from a platform

Feature lists answer "can it do the task once, in a demo." These six criteria answer "will it still be trustworthy after the fifth team is running unsupervised jobs on it." Apply each one to any platform on your shortlist before you commit time to a pilot.

Tool orchestration and execution surfaces (browser, terminal, files, connected apps)

Ask what the agent can actually act on, not just what it can talk about. A platform limited to chat and a handful of first-party plugins can explain a task; a platform with a real browser, a sandboxed terminal, persistent files, and structured connected-app actions can complete one. Real jobs mix surfaces: a research step needs the open web, a records update needs a structured app action rather than screen-scraping, and a file transform needs a terminal with somewhere durable to write the result.

How Construct answers: a live browser, a sandbox terminal, workspace files, and connected-app actions are available in the same task, and files persist between runs. Save anything a later run depends on to files, since browser and shell state end with the run. AI workflow automation shows how those surfaces combine into a recurring, scheduled procedure.

Human-in-the-loop controls and approval gates

The question is not whether a platform claims supervision. It is what specifically happens before an agent takes an external action a person did not directly request: can you interrupt a running task, does the agent stop to ask when something is ambiguous, and is there a mandatory approval step before it emails a customer or posts publicly. A platform that answers "yes, generally" to all three without naming the mechanism has not answered the question.

How Construct answers: you can watch a running task, interrupt it mid-turn, and answer when the agent stops to ask for a decision. Construct's workflows do not pause for approval yet, so for anything customer-facing, ask for drafts and send them yourself, and run a new job on demand a few times before moving it to the Calendar. See chat assistants vs AI employees for how that supervision model compares to a plain chat interface.

Audit trails and inspectable activity (and what "audit trail" should actually mean)

Vendors use "audit trail" loosely, and the gap between what it implies and what a product delivers matters once something goes wrong. A forensic audit log is an immutable, complete record of every operation, suitable for a compliance investigation. An activity summary is a readable record of what an agent did and why, suitable for an operator reviewing a day's work. Both are useful. They are not the same claim, and a buyer who needs the former should not accept a description of the latter at face value.

How Construct answers: it says plainly which one it provides. Activity records each action with a short reason for a limited window, and files, terminal transcripts, workflows, memories, and chat tool records stay visible in the workspace. That is a fast way to review a week of agent work; it is not a complete, immutable audit log, so a regulated team that needs one should keep its own records alongside (AI employee product guide). Ask every vendor which of the two they mean.

Connector coverage and custom integrations via MCP

Off-the-shelf integrations cover the common apps, but almost every real deployment eventually hits an internal system with no public integration. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has become the standard way agent platforms reach those systems: about 41% of surveyed software organizations already report agents connected through MCP servers in limited or broad production, according to Stacklok's 2026 survey as reported by Digital Applied (Digital Applied, MCP adoption statistics). Ask whether a platform supports custom MCP servers rather than only a fixed integration catalog.

How Construct answers: its live integration catalog covers common business apps, and a custom MCP server lets the hosted agent reach an internal system without waiting for first-party support: you implement the tool interface and the agent uses it. Construct vs building your own AI agent covers where that flexibility sits relative to a fully custom stack.

Persistent, correctable memory across sessions

A long chat history is not memory. The useful question is whether a platform can carry forward a stable fact, such as a preferred report format or a client contact, and whether you can correct that fact when it changes without wiping everything else the system knows. A platform that cannot distinguish "what was said" from "what is currently true" will eventually act on something that used to be accurate.

How Construct answers: it separates the raw episode from the durable assertion derived from it, versions corrections instead of silently overwriting them, and lets you inspect, correct, forget, or restore what it remembers. AI agent memory covers the provenance and correction model, including which sources are learned automatically and which you add explicitly.

Pricing model and real usage limits, not just a price tag

A published price answers less than it appears to. What predicts whether a plan fits a job is what gets metered: steps per task, scheduled tasks, concurrent background jobs, command runtime, and storage. Two platforms at the same monthly price can support very different workloads, and a plan that looks generous on paper can throttle a deep research task before it finishes.

How Construct answers: fixed monthly plans with published limits and no per-message billing. Lite at $9 includes 2 agents, 50 steps per task, and 3 scheduled tasks; Starter at $59 has 6x Lite's usage, 5 agents, 150 steps, and 10 scheduled tasks; Pro at $299 has 32x Lite's usage, 15 agents, up to 1,000 steps per task, 50 scheduled tasks, and bring-your-own-key support, with a 7-day trial. Each sandbox command can run for up to five minutes on every plan. See current plans, and ask any vendor for the equivalent numbers rather than the headline price alone.

Governance pressure is raising the bar: EU AI Act and "agent washing"

Two outside pressures are pushing evaluation criteria from nice-to-have to load-bearing. The first is regulatory. The EU AI Act's Article 14 requires high-risk AI systems to be designed so a human can effectively oversee them: monitor operation, intervene, and halt the system through a stop mechanism or equivalent procedure (EU AI Act, Article 14). The Act's full set of high-risk obligations, risk management, data governance, logging, transparency, human oversight, and cybersecurity, along with deployer obligations, were due to apply from August 2, 2026 (Legal Nodes, EU AI Act 2026 compliance timeline), but the AI Act Explorer now lists 2 December 2027 for high-risk systems under Annex III and 2 August 2028 under Annex I (AI Act Explorer, Article 14). Check the current date before you plan around either. A team whose agent work touches a use case the Act classifies as high-risk needs to treat human-in-the-loop controls and inspectable activity as compliance requirements, not product preferences.

The second pressure is a credibility problem inside the market itself. Gartner estimates that only about 130 of the thousands of vendors marketing "agentic AI" are genuinely agentic; the rest is what Gartner calls agent washing, existing chatbots, RPA, or assistants relabeled for a hotter category (Digital Applied, agent-washing definition and buyer's scorecard). That is why the checklist asks what a platform actually does rather than what it calls itself: a relabeled chatbot cannot orchestrate tools, hold correctable memory, or leave an inspectable trail.

Questions to ask a vendor before you pilot (and how Construct answers each one)

Bring these questions into a vendor call before you commit time to a pilot. Each maps to one of the six criteria above.

  1. What can the agent act on beyond chat, and what happens to that work when the session ends? Construct: a live browser, a sandbox terminal, connected-app actions, and its own email address, with workspace files persisting between sessions.
  2. What specifically stops the agent from doing something it should not? Construct: you can interrupt any running task, and its generated workspace apps declare an explicit allowlist of native capabilities, connected apps, and network origins; calls outside that allowlist are denied at runtime (How Construct builds internal tools).
  3. Is "audit trail" a forensic log or a readable summary? Construct: Activity is a readable record of each action with a short reason, stated as such, not an immutable forensic log.
  4. Can we reach a system you do not already integrate with? Construct: yes, through custom MCP servers, without waiting for first-party support.
  5. Can the agent be wrong about something and be corrected without losing everything else it knows? Construct: yes. It versions memory assertions, so a correction supersedes a stale fact while keeping the history of how it was learned.
  6. What is metered, beyond the sticker price? Construct: steps per task, scheduled tasks, agents, parallel background jobs, and storage, all published per plan. Ask for the same breakdown from any vendor you compare it against.

A 6-point scorecard you can apply to any AI agent platform

Score each criterion against a specific platform before a pilot, not after. A platform that cannot answer a row concretely, only in marketing language, should lose points on that row regardless of how polished the demo looked. The Construct column shows how it answers, so you can check each row yourself on Lite.

AI agent platform scorecard with Construct's answers

# Criterion Construct Weak signal Strong signal
1 Execution surfaces Browser, terminal, files, apps, and its own email in one task Chat plus a fixed plugin list Browser, terminal, files, and connected-app actions in one task
2 Memory Inspect, correct, forget, or restore versioned assertions Long chat history described as memory Correctable, provenance-tracked assertions separate from raw history
3 Pricing and limits Fixed monthly plans with steps, agents, schedules, jobs, and storage published Price with no usage detail Price plus steps, runtime, concurrency, and storage limits stated plainly
4 Connector coverage Live integration catalog plus custom MCP Fixed integration catalog only Native catalog plus custom MCP or an equivalent extension path
5 Audit trail Activity records each action with a short reason, stated as a readable record Vague "full audit trail" claim Explicit statement of whether it is forensic or a bounded summary
6 Human-in-the-loop controls Interrupt, ask-for-input, and drafts for review before anything is sent "Supervised" with no named mechanism Named interrupt, ask-for-input, and approval behavior, with stated gaps

A team piloting inbound lead qualification, for example, would run this scorecard against each shortlisted platform using the actual job: read a lead email, decide whether it qualifies, update the CRM, and send the team a summary. Score row 1 by watching which surface handles the CRM update. Score row 5 by asking, in writing, whether the vendor's activity record would hold up in a compliance review or only in a weekly stand-up. A platform that scores well on four rows and lower on two has told you exactly where the pilot needs extra supervision.

Already using another agent? Add Construct in 15 minutes

You do not need to cancel anything to run the checklist side by side. Take the job your current tool handles least reliably.

  1. Start on Lite for $9, or take the 7-day Pro trial if you want to test longer runs or your own model keys.
  2. Copy the instructions you gave your current agent into a Construct chat, and upload the source files to the workspace.
  3. Connect the apps the job needs from the integration catalog, or your own MCP server.
  4. Run it once and score the result against the six rows above.
  5. Put it on the Calendar so you can judge a week of scheduled runs, not a single demo.

There is no import from other agent platforms: write your rules into the first instruction and Construct saves them as memory you can read. Start with the AI employee explainer if the category is still new, and compare the market in our AI employee platforms roundup.

Construct answers every row of this scorecard concretely, starts at $9 a month, and keeps the work in a workspace your whole team can open, which makes it the platform to pilot first. Run your real job on it, score it honestly, and use the same six rows to judge anything else on your shortlist.

item.title: How Construct Builds Internal Tools in Your Workspace
item.description: Turn a repeated process into a private workspace app that Construct can build, validate, debug, and update while preserving the last successful build.
item.content:encoded:
Construct builds a private app for your team's repeated process, such as a request tracker, an intake form, a review queue, or a dashboard, inside the same workspace as the agent and files doing the work, from $9 a month. The usual alternatives are a spreadsheet that people copy values between, or a separate hosting project someone has to set up, secure, and maintain.

For founders and small teams, Construct is the faster way to get an internal tool. You describe the job in plain language; the agent writes the app, checks that it builds, and opens it in your desktop. The source stays in your files, permissions are declared up front, and a broken edit never takes the working version offline.

Why build it in Construct?

  • Describe the process, get the app. Construct writes the React and TypeScript, validates it, and opens it in the web desktop. No separate hosting project.
  • It lives beside the work. Source sits in Files under Apps/<app-id>/, and the app's data in AppData/<app-id>/, next to the reports and files it tracks.
  • Least privilege by default. Each app declares the capabilities, connected apps, and network origins it needs, and other calls are denied at runtime.
  • The last good build keeps running. A failed edit never replaces the working app while the agent repairs it.
  • The agent maintains it. Construct reads the app's own diagnostics, fixes the source, and validates again when something breaks.
  • Private to your workspace. Teammates with access can open it from the desktop, Launchpad, or Spotlight.

Start with the repeated process

The best request describes the work rather than prescribing a software architecture. For example:

  • "Build a research request tracker with an owner, priority, status, and link to the finished report."
  • "Turn this recurring launch checklist into an app the team can update."
  • "Create a dashboard for the JSON reports stored in this workspace."
  • "Build an intake form for customer-review requests and keep the queue in one place."

Construct can start from a list, form, dashboard, or blank interface. The agent creates the app package, writes the React and TypeScript source, declares the capabilities it needs, and validates the result. A successful build opens directly in the Construct web desktop instead of sending you to a separate hosting project.

The request still matters. "Build an operations dashboard" leaves important choices unresolved. "Show open research requests, let an operator assign an owner, and mark the linked report as reviewed" gives the agent a bounded workflow and a clear way to tell whether the app is useful.

Silent product demo: Construct writing, validating, and publishing a working internal app, then opening it in the product interface.

The app lives beside the work

A workspace app is not a hidden artifact. Its source lives under an Apps/<app-id>/ folder in Files, where it can be inspected and edited. After a successful build, the app appears as a private workspace install that can be reopened from the desktop, Launchpad, or Spotlight.

The app's durable state is kept separately under AppData/<app-id>/. That separation is important: changing the interface does not overwrite the records the app already manages. Rebuilding updates the code while existing app data remains in the workspace and counts against the normal workspace storage quota.

This model also makes the surrounding agent useful after launch. The same workspace contains the source, relevant files, conversations, and diagnostics. If the interface needs another field or a runtime error appears, the next task starts with the actual app rather than a screenshot and a vague bug report.

What a workspace app can do

The runtime is purpose-built for internal tools, which keeps each app close to its workspace job.

What a Construct workspace app supports

Capability Workspace-app support
React interface Yes
TypeScript and TSX Yes
Read or write workspace files With declared permission
App-scoped JSON state With declared Files permission
Call an allowed connected app With an explicit app allowlist
Make direct network requests To declared HTTPS origins
Packages The Construct SDK; arbitrary npm packages are not installed
Terminal and agent orchestration Run by the agent, not from the app UI
Visibility Private to your workspace; the public app registry has its own review process

The app UI receives a small Construct SDK for workspace files, app-scoped storage, notifications, window controls, and explicitly permitted calls. It does not inherit every tool available to the agent that authored it. The agent uses broader execution surfaces while building, but the finished interface runs with its own narrower contract.

Permissions are part of the design

An internal tool should not gain broad access simply because it was generated inside a trusted workspace. A workspace app declares the native capabilities, connected apps, and network origins it intends to use. Calls outside those allowlists are denied at runtime.

The platform also rechecks current workspace membership and permissions when the app makes a gateway call. File operations remain subject to the user's workspace access, and an app cannot use its file access to rewrite another app's package. Direct network access is limited to exact HTTPS origins rather than wildcard domains.

For a request tracker that only reads and writes workspace files, that can mean declaring Files access and nothing else. A tool that posts an approved record to a connected service needs that specific app target as well. The default is the smallest permission set that completes the job.

Validation, then verification

Before launch, Construct checks the package structure and manifest, follows relative imports, enforces package boundaries, compiles the TypeScript and JSX, and reports design findings. A successful validation creates an immutable artifact with a deterministic build ID and opens the app.

Validation proves the package builds under the workspace runtime. Click through the main actions once after a change, especially after changing permissions, storage behavior, or an external call, and Construct helps with the rest: it captures console, network, gateway, and runtime-error diagnostics from workspace apps, inspects recent errors, repairs the source, validates again, and asks you to verify the changed behavior. The loop is closer to maintaining a small internal product than generating a disposable code snippet.

Draft changes do not replace the last good build

A successful build becomes the current runtime artifact. Later source edits mark the app as having draft changes, but opening the app continues to run the last successful build until the new source validates.

If validation fails, the working artifact is not replaced. Cancelling an edit also leaves both the source and prior build in place. The desktop shows whether an app is ready, has draft changes, or has never built successfully. This is a last-good-build fallback that protects the working tool while a repair is in progress, rather than a browsable history of every build.

Internal tool or workflow?

Not every repeated process needs an interface. Use a workspace app when people need to view, enter, filter, or review state. Use a Construct workflow when the main value is running a known sequence of agent steps, connected-app actions, and notifications. Use a scheduled agent job when the process should run in the background without waiting for someone to open a screen.

The two support the same operation. A workspace app provides the queue and review surface, files hold durable records, and a scheduled job prepares new work. Automation still runs through the execution surfaces and permissions designed for it, so the app UI stays a focused interface.

Before you start: where workspace apps fit

Good fits are narrow tools with a clear operator and a durable workspace context:

  • Intake forms and review queues
  • Checklists for repeated operations
  • Lightweight trackers over workspace records
  • Dashboards for files or app-scoped JSON data
  • Focused interfaces over an explicitly allowed connected service
  • Small utilities that make an existing workflow easier to run and inspect

A workspace app is an internal interface for one workspace, not a public product. For a customer-facing site, a product that needs the wider npm ecosystem, or a system with its own infrastructure and security controls, keep a dedicated hosting stack, and let Construct build the internal tools around it.

Already tracking this in a spreadsheet? Move it in 15 minutes

item.description: Zapier runs a fixed trigger-action recipe. See how an AI agent plans its own steps instead, with a side-by-side of the same recurring workflow built both ways.
item.content:encoded:
Construct gives you an AI agent that plans its own steps across your apps, a live browser, workspace files, and its own email address from $9 a month, with 3 scheduled jobs included on Lite. Zapier runs a fixed trigger-action recipe instead: every step is wired in advance, a Zap caps out at 100 steps, and paid plans start at $29.99 a month for 750 tasks (Zapier, Zap limits; Zapier, pricing).

For founders and small teams whose recurring work involves reading, judgment, or research, Construct is the better choice. You describe the outcome once instead of building a tree of Paths, the agent handles the cases nobody wired for, and every finished file stays in a workspace your team can open next week. Already running Zaps? Keep the simple ones and give Construct the jobs that keep falling through.

Why choose Construct over a Zap?

  • One job description instead of a tree of Paths. Tell Construct what a finished result looks like and it works out the order of operations at run time. Nobody has to anticipate every branch up front.
  • Judgment where the rules run out. A lead that does not match the qualification rules, or an email that needs a judgment call, gets read and handled instead of falling through a filter.
  • Reaches sites with no integration. When a step needs a website or a script, Construct uses a live browser or a sandbox terminal alongside its live integration catalog and your own MCP tools.
  • Work that outlives the run. Reports and spreadsheets are saved to workspace files as the agent produces them, so a run that stops at step 30 still leaves steps 1 to 29 behind.
  • Memory you can correct. Construct remembers your qualification criteria and report format between runs, and you can open, fix, or forget any stored fact.
  • $9 a month to start. Lite includes 2 agents, 50 steps per task, and 3 scheduled tasks. Starter at $59 raises that to 5 agents, 150 steps, and 10 scheduled tasks.

How a Zap works

A Zap starts with a trigger: a new row in a spreadsheet, a new email in Gmail, a new deal in a CRM. Optional filter steps decide whether the run continues, and action steps carry out each following task, such as creating a record or sending a message. Every step in that chain is wired in advance, and the Zap runs it in the order it was built.

Zap workflows cap out at 100 steps total, including every step nested inside Paths, and Zapier does not support two-way syncing between apps: workflows only run in one direction (Zapier, Zap limits). A workflow that needs to read a reply, weigh a few possible responses, and pick among them has to be pre-built as a tree of Paths and filters for every case its builder thought to include. A case outside that tree falls through.

Zapier also offers a Human in the Loop step that pauses a running Zap to request approval, an edit, or missing data from a reviewer before the workflow continues (Zapier, Human in the Loop).

How Construct plans the steps at run time

An AI agent inverts the build order. Instead of wiring trigger, filter, and action steps in advance, you give it an outcome and it works out the path. Zapier has added its own agent product built on the same idea, pointed at business data and a goal (Zapier, Agents). Construct starts there: you assign a goal, and the agent chooses among live browser runs, a sandbox terminal, workspace files, and the apps in its live integration catalog, deciding the order of operations as the job unfolds.

You stay in control while it works. Construct's Activity feed records each action with a short reason, chat keeps the tool records, and you can interrupt a job mid-run or answer when the agent asks for missing information. Construct's workflows do not pause for approval yet, so for anything customer-facing, ask for drafts and send them yourself once you have checked them.

Construct also carries context forward. Workspace files and inspectable long-term memory persist across sessions, so next week's run starts from this week's results and the rules you already explained.

Construct Starter $59 6x Lite usage, up to 5 agents, 150 steps per task, 10 scheduled tasks
Construct Pro $299 32x Lite usage, up to 15 agents, up to 1,000 steps per task, 50 scheduled tasks, your keys
Zapier Professional $29.99 750 tasks, unlimited multi-step Zaps
Zapier Team $103.50 2,000 tasks

Sources: Construct pricing and Zapier pricing. Zapier prices were current as of this post's original publish date and can change; check Zapier's pricing page for the latest figures. Construct is priced per plan, not per seat: a team workspace has no member limit, and everyone's work draws on the owner's plan.

The same recurring workflow, two ways

A concrete example makes the difference easier to see: a new lead lands in Gmail, needs to be qualified, gets logged in the CRM, and the team gets a summary.

Stage Run by Construct Built in Zapier
Build effort One job description after the inbox, CRM connection, and schedule are set up One multi-step Zap with Paths for anticipated cases, tested and maintained as its rules change
Qualification The agent reads the email in context and judges whether the lead qualifies, including cases the rules did not anticipate A Filter step and a Paths branch encode the qualification rules in advance: company size field, keyword match, domain check
CRM update The agent updates the CRM directly, and can check the sender's site or prior email history to fill a gap the message itself does not answer A CRM action step maps fields from the trigger payload; a missing or unrecognized field needs its own Path to handle
Summary The agent emails a summary from its own address, in its own words, including why it judged the lead qualified A Slack action step posts a fixed message template to a channel
Start A scheduled job checks the inbox for new leads on the interval you choose A Zap watches Gmail for new messages matching a label or search filter

The Construct version handles the leads that do not fit the pattern, and its reasoning is written into every summary. It runs as a scheduled inbox check rather than firing the instant a message arrives, which suits lead follow-up measured in hours rather than seconds.

Silent product demo: Construct building and running a reusable workflow in the product interface, with agent steps, connected apps, and notifications.

Where agent-based automation is headed

The gap this closes shows up in how much unstructured coordination work still sits on people's calendars. Knowledge workers spend about 60% of their time on "work about work," communicating about tasks, hunting for information, and switching between apps, rather than on the skilled work itself, according to Asana's Anatomy of Work Index, based on a global survey of more than 10,000 knowledge workers (Asana, Anatomy of Work Index). Much of that time goes to exactly the kind of judgment calls and cross-app handoffs a fixed trigger-action recipe cannot absorb.

Analyst research points the same direction. Gartner predicts that 40% of enterprise applications will feature task-specific AI agents by the end of 2026, up from less than 5% in 2025. "AI agents are evolving rapidly, progressing from basic assistants embedded in enterprise applications today to task-specific agents by 2026 and ultimately multiagent ecosystems by 2029," said Anushree Verma, Sr Director Analyst at Gartner (Gartner, press release). Zapier's own move toward Agents and Human in the Loop steps fits the same pattern: even a platform built on fixed automations is adding room for a system to plan.

item.title: AI Agent Memory You Can Control
item.description: Give an AI agent persistent memory with provenance, corrections, temporal context, and controls to inspect, update, forget, or restore what it knows.
item.content:encoded:
Construct gives your AI agent long-term memory you can open, correct, forget, and restore, included on every plan from $9 a month. A long chat history only records what was said: it cannot tell an agent which fact is still true, and you cannot fix one wrong fact without losing the thread around it.

For founders and small teams running recurring work, Construct's memory is the better foundation. Every remembered fact keeps its source, a correction replaces a stale fact without erasing how it was learned, and nothing it remembers is hidden from you. Your recurring jobs start from context instead of from a fresh explanation.

Why do this in Construct?

  • Memory you can read. The Memories app lets you search everything Construct remembers and see the evidence behind each item.
  • Corrections, not silent overwrites. A corrected fact supersedes the old one, and the history of the change stays visible.
  • Forget and restore. Remove a fact that should not persist, and bring it back if it was removed by mistake.
  • Sources stay attached. Each remembered fact keeps the episode it came from, so you can trace why the agent believes it.
  • Works with files and schedules. Memory carries the context a scheduled workflow assumes, and files hold the documents themselves.
  • Included from $9 a month. Lite includes 2 agents, 50 steps per task, and 3 scheduled tasks; Pro has a 7-day free trial.

Why long-term agent memory matters

A useful work agent needs more than the messages currently visible in chat. It should remember stable preferences, ongoing projects, important people, and prior decisions when they are relevant to a new task. Without that continuity, every recurring workflow begins with the same explanation and the same avoidable mistakes.

Construct recalls relevant context before a turn and saves useful information after successful work. Source episodes remain separate from the assertions the memory system derives from them, so remembered information keeps its origin rather than becoming an unexplained fact.

That separation is the part most worth understanding. An episode is the raw thing that happened: a conversation turn, a web search, a fetched page. An assertion is the durable claim derived from it, such as a preferred report format or a customer's current role. Keeping the two apart means a remembered fact can be traced back to the moment it was learned, which is what makes a correction meaningful rather than cosmetic.

Three kinds of memory, often confused

"Memory" gets used for three different mechanisms, and the distinction decides what you can actually rely on.

Context window, retrieval, and long-term memory compared

Mechanism What it holds How long it lasts
Long-term memory Durable assertions with provenance and validity Across tasks until corrected or forgotten
Retrieval Documents fetched to answer a specific question Only for that lookup
Context window The current turn and recent messages One conversation, then gone

A chat product with a long history is not the same as an agent with long-term memory. History preserves what was said; memory preserves what is currently true, and can be changed when it stops being true. Construct's Memories app manages the first row.

What Construct learns automatically, and what you add yourself

Construct learns automatically from conversation episodes and successful public web search or fetch evidence. Facts from private surfaces, such as uploaded files, connected-app results, terminal output, and live browser runs, are added when you or the agent save them explicitly.

That keeps memory smaller and more trustworthy. Private surfaces often contain credentials, customer data, and half-finished work nobody meant to promote into durable memory, so Construct leaves the choice to you.

How each source reaches Construct's memory

Source How it reaches memory
Conversation episodes Automatically
Successful public web search/fetch Automatically
Uploaded files Add explicitly
Private connected-app results Add explicitly
Terminal output Add explicitly
Live browser runs Add explicitly

The practical rule: if a fact arrived through a private surface and a future task depends on it, ask Construct to remember it, or add it in the Memories app.

A worked example: the recurring client report

A concrete case shows how the pieces fit. Suppose a monthly performance report goes to a client's operations lead.

First run. You explain the audience, the sections they care about, and that figures should be quoted to two decimal places. Construct produces the report, and the useful parts of that exchange become assertions with their originating episode attached.

Second run. You assign the same job without repeating the setup. Construct recalls the format and audience before starting, so the run begins from context rather than from explanation.

Something changes. The client's operations lead moves on and a new contact takes over. You correct the assertion about who receives the report. The old assertion is superseded and its history remains visible, so a later question about why earlier reports were addressed differently still has an answer.

Something needs to go. A pricing detail shared in confidence should not persist. You forget that assertion. If it turns out to have been removed in error, it can be restored.

The durable output here is not just the reports. It is a small set of inspectable assertions that make each subsequent run cheaper to start, plus a record of how those assertions changed.

Corrections instead of silent overwrites

Facts change. A customer changes roles, a project gets renamed, or a preference that was once correct stops applying. Construct versions memory assertions and tracks when information is valid. A correction can supersede an older assertion without erasing the history that explains how the system learned it.

This temporal model helps the agent distinguish current context from old context. It also makes a correction auditable: you can see the updated assertion instead of hoping a new embedding happens to outrank the old one.

The failure mode this avoids is worth naming. In a system that stores memories as undifferentiated text and retrieves by similarity, a corrected fact and its outdated predecessor both remain in the store, competing for retrieval. The agent may surface either one depending on how a question is phrased, and there is no reliable way to tell which it used. Versioned assertions with validity windows make the current value explicit rather than probabilistic.

Memory controls for people

The Memories app lets you search and inspect what Construct remembers. You can add an explicit memory, correct an existing one, forget information, or restore something removed by mistake. Pending or unreviewed information can be excluded from automatic recall until it is safe to use.

  • Search memories and inspect supporting context
  • Correct stale or inaccurate assertions
  • Forget information that should no longer be recalled
  • Restore previously forgotten information

Silent product demo: Construct's Memories app showing the preferences and procedures the agent has learned, with the evidence behind each one, so you can review, correct, or forget them.

Reviewing memory occasionally is worth the few minutes it takes, particularly after a project changes shape. Assertions learned during a since-abandoned approach are the most common source of confidently wrong recall.

Memory connects work across time

Memory becomes more valuable when it works with the rest of the workspace. During a task, Construct combines recalled context with files, scheduled jobs, workflows, inbox threads, and connected applications. A weekly report remembers the audience and preferred format; an inbox task uses an explicitly remembered customer preference; a research job builds on earlier findings without starting over.

This is also why memory and reusable workflows complement each other. A workflow encodes the steps of a procedure; memory carries the context those steps assume. A workflow without memory needs its assumptions restated every run, and remembered context without a workflow leaves the sequence to be reconstructed each time.

Before you start: what belongs in memory

Memory works best for facts that are stable, reused, and expensive to restate. The workspace has a better home for everything else.

  • Large documents belong in workspace files, which persist and can be reopened directly. Memory holds the fact that a document matters, not its contents.
  • Secrets and credentials go through connected-app authentication rather than being stated in a conversation that may become an episode.
  • Fast-changing values such as live metrics are better fetched at run time, since a remembered figure is correct only until the next change.
  • One-off context that will not recur does not need to be durable, and an uncluttered memory recalls better than a crowded one.

Already using ChatGPT memory or another agent? Move your context in 15 minutes

  1. Start on Lite for $9, or take the 7-day Pro trial.
  2. Write down the standing facts your current assistant relies on: audiences, formats, key contacts, and rules.
  3. Paste them into a Construct chat and ask it to remember them, then check each one in the Memories app.
  4. Run one recurring job and confirm it starts from that context.
  5. Put it on the Calendar so the job runs every week with the same remembered setup.

There is no import of another product's memory: writing the facts out once is the import, and every one of them stays readable and correctable in Construct.

Which should you choose?

Choose Construct for agent memory you control. It starts at $9 a month, keeps the source of every remembered fact, lets you correct, forget, or restore any item, and works alongside files, workflows, and schedules so recurring jobs start from the right context every time.

Give Construct the recurring report you explain from scratch every month: describe the audience, sections, and format once, let it produce the first report, then open the Memories app and check what it saved. Next month, assign the job in one line. Start on Lite at $9, or try Pro free for seven days.

item.title: AI Workflow Automation
item.description: Create reusable linear AI workflows, run them on demand, or schedule recurring work across files, live browser runs, native email, and connected business apps.
item.content:encoded:
Construct turns a job that worked once into a saved workflow that runs from its Calendar, server-side with your laptop closed, from $9 a month with 3 scheduled tasks on Lite. Trigger-action tools need every step wired in advance, so the moment a job needs research, a rewritten summary, or a page that changed its layout, the recipe stops and a person finishes it by hand.

For founders and small teams, Construct is the better way to automate recurring knowledge work. An agent step handles the parts that need judgment, connected-app actions and notifications handle the rest, and every run leaves files and history you can open. You build the workflow from a run that already succeeded, so it is a record of working steps rather than a guess.

Why do this in Construct?

  • Encode after it works. Do the job once in chat, confirm the output, then save the steps as a workflow.
  • Agent steps where rules break. An agent step reads the situation and decides what to do, so a changed page or an odd input does not stop the run.
  • Every surface in one procedure. Connected-app actions, web research, a live browser, a sandbox terminal, workspace files, and its own email address.
  • Runs with your laptop closed. Calendar schedules run server-side: 3 scheduled tasks on Lite, 10 on Starter, 50 on Pro.
  • Published versions stay put. Editing a workflow does not silently rewrite a run that already started.
  • Anyone on the team can run it. Team workspaces have Owner, Admin, and Member roles and no member limit, so coverage no longer depends on the person who wrote the steps.

From one good run to a reusable procedure

AI workflow automation is useful when a procedure contains research, judgment, writing, or tool use that cannot be reduced to a fixed data mapping. Construct combines durable workflow steps with an agent that handles those less predictable parts.

A workflow can include agent work, connected-app actions, and in-app notifications. Published versions are preserved so a future edit does not silently change a run that already started. Run history makes the procedure easier to inspect and improve over time.

The sequence that works is to do the job once conversationally, confirm the output is right, and only then encode it. A workflow written before the job has ever succeeded is a guess about the steps. A workflow written afterwards is a record of steps already known to produce the result you wanted.

A worked example: the Monday competitor digest

Consider a recurring task: every Monday, check five competitors' pricing pages, note anything that changed since last week, and save a dated summary for the team.

Run it once. Ask Construct to gather the current pricing for each competitor and summarize it. It uses web search and fetch for public pages, and a live browser run for any page that needs interaction. You review the output and correct the framing.

Encode it. Save the procedure as a workflow: an agent step that gathers and compares pricing and saves a dated summary to Files, and a notification step so you see the run even when nobody is watching the workspace.

Schedule it. Add it to Construct's Calendar as a recurring Monday job. The scheduler runs it server-side and reconciles missed or delayed work rather than depending on an open browser tab.

Inspect it. Each run leaves step results, retry information, and Activity summaries. Agent steps link back to their chat sessions, so a week where the summary looked wrong can be opened and read rather than guessed at.

The durable output is a versioned procedure, a dated summary each week, and a run history that makes the procedure improvable. When a competitor redesigns a pricing page and the step starts returning less useful results, the run history is where that shows up.

Silent product demo: Construct building and running a reusable workflow in the product interface, with agent steps, connected apps, and notifications.

Run now or put it on the Calendar

Construct's Calendar is a scheduler for agent work and workflows. Create a one-time job, define a recurring schedule, run it immediately, or cancel it from the same workspace. Scheduled runs happen server-side, so they do not depend on an open browser tab or your laptop being on.

This makes recurring operating work practical: weekly market research, an inbox summary, a customer follow-up list, or a report assembled from several connected systems. Google Calendar can be connected as an external app, but Construct's native Calendar controls when agent jobs run.

Workflow runs start on demand or from the Calendar. For a workflow that should react to incoming mail, schedule an inbox check at the interval you choose; the agent reads what arrived since the last run and handles it.

Use the right execution surface

Each step can use the surface that fits the job. Structured app actions are best for reliable updates. Web search and fetch handle public research. A live browser covers interactive sites, including logins completed during that run. The sandbox terminal processes files, runs scripts, and generates artifacts, with files saved under the workspace persisting after the run.

Which Construct surface fits each workflow step

Step needs Best surface Where the result lives
Update a record in a business app Connected-app action In that app
Research a public topic Web search and fetch Saved files or memory
Use a site that needs interaction Live browser run Files the step saves during the run
Transform a file or run a script Sandbox terminal Workspace files
Tell someone the run happened In-app notification In the workspace

The right-hand column matters more than it first appears. Live browser runs and shell state exist for the duration of the run, so anything a later step or a later week depends on should be written to workspace files while the run is in progress. Construct saves finished work as it goes, so a run that stops at step 30 still leaves steps 1 to 29 behind.

  • Collect sources and create a cited brief
  • Read messages and update a connected system
  • Process a file and save the transformed output
  • Create an in-app notification, or post through a connected app

Inspect every run

Workflow automation should be debuggable. Construct keeps run state, step results, retry information, and Activity summaries. You can open resulting files and review connected-app actions; agent steps also link to their chat sessions, and the agent can ask for missing information during interactive work.

Construct's workflows do not pause for approval yet, so for a workflow that posts publicly, emails customers, or updates shared records, have it save drafts for a person to send, and run it manually a few times before it goes on a schedule. Reviewing the first several runs is the cheapest way to catch a step that behaves differently than intended.

Before you start: designing for linear runs

Construct workflows run as a straight sequence of steps, which keeps them readable: a sequence you can walk, not a graph you have to debug. A few patterns follow.

  • Conditional work belongs inside an agent step. The agent reads the situation and decides what to do; the workflow itself does not fork.
  • Multi-stage procedures can be split into separate workflows scheduled at different times, with workspace files carrying state between them.
  • Approval-gated work works best as an on-demand workflow that a person starts after reviewing, or as a scheduled run that saves drafts.
  • Jobs that run once are quicker to assign in chat than to encode, and a procedure still changing weekly is worth running in chat until its shape settles.

Already using Zapier or Make? Add Construct in 15 minutes

Keep your existing automations. Move the one that keeps needing a person to finish it.

  1. Start on Lite for $9, or take the 7-day Pro trial for longer runs and more scheduled tasks.
  2. Describe the outcome in a Construct chat, pasting in the steps and rules from your current flow.
  3. Connect the apps the job needs from the integration catalog.
  4. Run it once and check the result in Files.
  5. Save it as a workflow and put it on the Calendar.

There is no import from other automation tools: the job description and the saved workflow replace the flow. The Construct vs Zapier comparison covers where each model fits, and AI agent vs Zapier automation walks the same workflow built both ways.

When might a trigger-action tool still fit?

  • Purely deterministic, high-volume mappings with no judgment step.
  • Work that must react within seconds of an event.
  • A flow that needs built-in branching, delays, or fan-out today.

For a procedure that is stable, repeated, and needs enough judgment that a fixed mapping would be brittle, Construct is the better fit.

Start your first workflow

Choose Construct for recurring work that needs judgment. It starts at $9 a month, builds the workflow from a run that already worked, runs it server-side on a schedule, and keeps every result where your team can open it.

Give Construct the Monday competitor digest: list the five pricing pages, ask for a dated summary of what changed, check the first result, save it as a workflow, and put it on the Calendar, where it uses one of Lite's 3 scheduled tasks. Start on Lite at $9, or try Pro free for seven days.

Construct uses live browser runs, a sandbox terminal, workspace files, and connected applications to perform those steps and returns with the finished artifact, chat tool records, and Activity summaries.

That gap shows up in three places:

  1. Unified persistence: chat products may offer history, projects, files, or memory depending on the product and plan; Construct keeps files, procedures, schedules, and inspectable memory in one workspace.
  2. Execution surfaces: available chat tools vary by product and plan, while Construct combines connected apps with live browser runs, a sandbox terminal, native email, and workspace files in the same task.
  3. Inspectable work: Construct keeps Activity summaries, chat tool records, sent messages, connected-app updates, and workspace files together after the job is done.

The same request, handled two ways

Take a request that sounds simple: "Check whether any of our top ten accounts have gone quiet this month, and draft follow-ups for the ones that have."

In Construct. The agent reads the accounts through a connected-app action, compares against the figures saved in workspace files from last month, drafts the follow-ups, and either sends them from its own inbox or leaves them for review. The files, the sent messages, and the Activity summary stay in the workspace. Next month, the same job runs from the Calendar.

In a chat assistant. You export account activity yourself, paste it in, and get back an analysis and draft follow-ups. You did the data gathering, you will do the sending, and next month the whole exchange starts over from an empty thread.

The drafted text might be comparable. The difference is how much of the surrounding work a person still has to do, and whether anything is left behind that makes the next run cheaper.

Repeating work without rebuilding it

Construct's native Calendar schedules one-time or recurring agent jobs and workflow runs, and they run server-side whether or not anyone is online. A workflow can combine agent reasoning, connected-app actions, and in-app notifications, then keep run history for inspection. Control without constant monitoring

Construct is built for supervised execution. You can inspect outputs, interrupt a running turn, answer a question when the agent needs a decision, and review or correct long-term memory. Construct's workflows do not pause for approval yet, so for anything customer-facing, ask for drafts and send them yourself once you have checked them.
